content: A reflex action is an automatic, involuntary neuromuscular response triggered by a specific stimulus. In humans, reflex actions are typically mediated through a reflex arc, although this is not universally true in other animals or in less formal uses of the term reflex. A reflex action, or reflex, functions as a biological control system that connects a stimulus to a response via the reflex arc. Reflexes can be innate or acquired. For instance, when a person steps on a sharp object, specialized sensory receptors in the skin of the foot generate a nociceptive stimulus. This stimulus is transmitted via an afferent nerve to the spinal cord. Within the spinal cord, the stimulus is often processed by an interneuron, which generates an immediate motor response to withdraw the foot from the painful object. This withdrawal occurs even as the sensation of pain is being transmitted to the brain, where it is consciously perceived and cognitively evaluated. Reflexes are commonly assessed during neurological examinations to evaluate the integrity and functionality of the central and peripheral nervous systems. Reflexes can also be trained, such as through repetitive motor actions during sports practice or through the association of stimuli with autonomic responses during classical conditioning. The reaction time, or latency, of a reflex is the interval between the onset of a stimulus and the organism's response. In humans, the reaction time to visual stimuli typically ranges from 150 to 300 milliseconds. Human reflex actions include several categories: Tendon Reflexes and Stretch Reflexes Deep tendon reflexes provide critical information about the health of the central and peripheral nervous systems. Generally, diminished reflexes suggest peripheral nervous system issues, while exaggerated reflexes indicate central nervous system problems. Examples include: Biceps stretch reflex (C5, C6) Brachioradialis reflex (C5, C6) Triceps stretch reflex (C7, C8) Patellar reflex or knee-jerk reflex (L3, L4) Achilles reflex (S1, S2) Plantar reflex or Babinski reflex (L5, S1, S2) While these reflexes are mechanically stimulated, the H-reflex is an analogous reflex elicited electrically, and the tonic vibration reflex is triggered by vibration. Reflexes Involving Cranial Nerves Certain reflexes are mediated by cranial nerves, which play a role in various sensory and motor functions. Reflexes in Infants Only Newborns exhibit a range of primitive reflexes that are not present in adults. These include: Asymmetrical tonic neck reflex (ATNR) Grasp reflex Hand-to-mouth reflex Moro reflex (startle reflex) Sucking reflex Symmetrical tonic neck reflex (STNR) Tonic labyrinthine reflex (TLR) Other Reflexes Additional reflexes observed in the human nervous system include: Anocutaneous reflex Crossed extensor reflex Escape reflex Jaw jerk reflex Mammalian diving reflex Oculocardiac reflex Optokinetic reflex Photic sneeze reflex Scratch reflex Withdrawal reflex Processes such as breathing, digestion, and the maintenance of the heartbeat can also be considered reflex actions under certain definitions of the term.
